analysis.one_liner: Creates a commission with power to let federal regulations lapse unless it re-approves each one.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee; no House or Senate vote was ever taken before the 1993-94 Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set expiration dates on every federal regulation. A new nine-member commission, appointed by the President, would review each rule under criteria like cost, duplication, and burdens on business. Any rule the commission did not affirmatively approve would automatically stop being enforced — existing rules after seven years, new rules after three. It was introduced in November 1993, sent to two House committees, and died there without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses subject to federal rules — on pollution, workplace safety, consumer protection, finance, and more — would gain, because every rule would face a standing threat of automatic expiration unless a politically appointed commission re-approved it. Companies that find rules costly or outdated could press the commission during its review process.

how_it_helps.text: Every existing regulation would expire seven years after enactment unless the commission affirmatively authorized it to continue, and new rules would expire after three years [S3].

The commission would judge rules by criteria including whether benefits exceed costs, whether rules impede competition, whether information requirements can be reduced for small businesses, and whether rules rely on market mechanisms [S3].
Each agency would have to review its own rules and report to the commission, and a Regulatory Review Officer would be placed inside every agency to enforce compliance [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who depend on federal rules — clean air and water standards, food and drug safety, workplace and financial protections — would bear the risk, since any rule a busy nine-member commission failed to re-approve would simply stop applying. Agencies would also lose control of their own rulebooks, and taxpayers would fund a new commission and new review staff in every agency.

drawbacks.text: The default is expiration: a rule stays in force only if the commission acts. With the federal government issuing thousands of rules, a small commission reviewing them on a rolling schedule could let important protections lapse simply by missing a deadline [S3].

Judicial review would be sharply limited — challenges to a commission decision would have to be filed within 30 days — leaving affected parties little recourse if a protective rule were terminated [S3].

A fair objection in the bill's favor: regulations do accumulate, become outdated, and overlap, and the bill's criteria include cutting duplicate paperwork, especially for small businesses [S3]. But critics of sunset schemes have long argued that automatic expiration gives regulated industries repeated chances to kill rules they dislike, rather than requiring Congress to repeal them openly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some housekeeping value is real — rules do go stale and duplicate each other, and regular review could cut burdens on small businesses. But the design puts a thumb heavily on the side of elimination: inaction kills a rule rather than preserving it, and the review criteria weigh costs, competition, and industry conditions alongside public health and safety. The main effect would be to make every federal protection permanently negotiable in front of a politically appointed commission.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to subcommittees, and neither committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Chapman introduced the bill on November 22, 1993, and it was referred jointly to the House Judiciary and Government Operations committees [S1][S5].
Five members cosponsored it — four Democrats and one Republican [S4].
In early December 1993 it was sent to the Subcommittee on Legislation and National Security and the Subcommittee on Administrative Law and Governmental Relations, where it stayed [S5].
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate action is recorded; the bill died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public that relies on federal health, safety, environmental, and financial rules is better off, since no existing protection was put at risk of automatic expiration. Agencies also avoided losing final authority over their own rulebooks.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's tiny sponsor group was mixed-party — five cosponsors split four Democrats to one Republican — and no votes were ever taken, so no partisan pattern can be measured.

industries.industry: Regulated industries generally (manufacturing, energy, finance, and other businesses subject to federal rules)
industries.note: Every federal rule would face automatic expiration unless a politically appointed commission re-approved it, giving regulated businesses a standing tool to press for rules they dislike to lapse. The public bears the cost if protective rules disappear.

The bill's review criteria explicitly include reducing information and paperwork requirements, particularly for small businesses, and eliminating duplicate or overlapping rules. This is the group with the most plausible genuine benefit.

Agencies would lose final authority over their own rules — a commission could terminate regulations agencies wrote to carry out their statutory missions — and each agency would have to fund a new review officer and ongoing reporting duties.
